summary: Hearth (Hear + Earth) turns NASA’s Earth visualizations into sound, so people who cannot see them can still explore them. A scan line crosses each NASA map and whatever it crosses plays: north sounds higher and in the left ear, and more light, dust, pollution or warmth sounds louder and fuller. Eight tracks cover night lights, air quality, ocean currents, carbon dioxide, lightning, aerosols, sea temperature and El Niño. Hearth answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing NASA’s Earth Information Center visuals with sound generated live from their data. It is built for blind and low-vision listeners first: a first-time screen reader user can use it alone, by keyboard. This matters because NASA’s picture of our changing planet should belong to everyone, not only to people who can see it.
details:
What it does: Hearth is a web page with eight tracks, each made from one NASA Scientific Visualization Studio visualization. Press Play and a scan line crosses the map, west to east (on the sea temperature track, north to south). Each track has its own sound: ringing notes for bright cities, a drone that turns sour where the air is worst, four different winds for smoke, dust, sea salt and sulfate, an orchestra and harp for lightning, chords that gain higher voices as the sea gets warmer, and rising or falling notes for El Niño’s warm and cool seas. A 3D globe and a flat map show exactly what you hear, never more.

How it works: A Python pipeline reads NASA’s own video frames and maps. Each pixel’s colour is matched to the colour key NASA prints on the visualization and turned back into a value, for example degrees Celsius on NASA’s 0–32 °C sea temperature key. Values are averaged into a 3-degree grid (120 × 60 cells) with one fixed scale per track, then written as a “score” that a validator checks. In the browser, Tone.js plays the score live. Nothing is uploaded.

Accessibility: Every action works by keyboard and screen reader with native controls. The page says what to press next. W (“Where am I?”) tells you the track, map, scan-line position and last note. D describes the map. Every sound has an example button that explains it. There are settings for mono, speed and volume, and a WAV download. It is tested by keyboard, with automated accessibility rules, and at seven screen widths.

Benefits and goals: blind and low-vision people get independent access to NASA Earth science, and everyone gets a new, memorable way to notice patterns such as storms swinging north and south with the seasons. Next steps: testing with blind listeners in Mongolia, a Mongolian-language version, and more NASA visualizations.

Tools: Python (NumPy, OpenCV, PyYAML, ffmpeg) for the data pipeline; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the site; Tone.js for sound; esbuild; Playwright and axe-core for tests; hosted on Vercel. Code: https://github.com/atuuuuuuu/earth-jukebox

Limits: values are read from the colours of NASA’s visualizations, so most are relative levels rather than satellite units (sea temperature and El Niño are read in °C). NASA’s lightning movie has no dates, so it is played as 14 equal parts.

El Niño (SVS 5176): in September 2026, the sea in the Niño 3.4 region of the equatorial Pacific reads +2.05 °C from NASA's pixels. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center reports +2.1 °C. Every month of 2025 stays below the El Niño line, and 2026 crosses it in May.

Night lights (SVS 5313): from 2012 to 2023, the world's light grows 24% and India's grows 86%. Kyiv loses light after 2021, as NASA's own change map shows.

Aerosols (SVS 5669): in all six events NASA describes, the aerosol NASA names is the strongest one we read. Hurricane Erin reads as sea salt, Saharan dust as dust, Kilauea and Etna as sulfate, and the African and Spanish fires as smoke.

Gulf Stream (SVS 5425): the directions measured from NASA's flow lines run north off Miami, northeast off Georgia and east off the Carolinas. The fastest water is about 115 km off Cape Canaveral, inside the stream.

One Blind Tester quoted "It's very easy to access and we're happy to feel the earth with sound."
